slides.title: Should Parcelbird launch its own quick-commerce service in 2027?
Key questions

claims.claim: Should Parcelbird launch Parcelbird Now, its own 15-minute grocery delivery service, in 2027 while reaching profit within its $12.0M of cash and keeping 12 months of runway?
evidence: Sub-questions: 1 Is quick commerce a market in which a new regional entrant can make money? 2 Can Parcelbird Now make money on each order once store costs are counted? 3 Did Columbus show the density and loyalty the model needs, at an affordable cost? 4 Can the launch be funded with 12 months of runway, and is there a better use of the cash? 5 What should Parcelbird do in 2027, and when would it revisit an own service?
Decision maker: The board (two founders and two investors)

Success criteria: A path to profitability within the current $12.0M of cash, with no new funding round; At least 12 months of runway at all times; Contribution profit per order by month 18, as the founders' model claims
Timing: Board meeting, January 2027
Out of scope: Cities beyond the three planned; A new funding round; The software product roadmap

slides.title: The market grows, but no one profits

claims.claim: Profit is missing: both incumbents lose money per order on average, and the regional player is closing cities

claims.claim: "nobody owns the Midwest" is not tested

slides.title: Next steps

normalized.recommendation: Do not launch Parcelbird Now in 2027; grow the software business instead. Decide against the launch in January, fund four software hires (2 engineers and 2 sales staff) and sell store-based fast delivery to grocers; reopen the question only when customer sites pass four tests.

alternatives_considered.option: Launch Parcelbird Now (own 15-minute dark-store grocery delivery, nine stores in Columbus, Indianapolis and Kansas City)
alternatives_considered.treatment: Rejected: "Do not launch" — no path to profit on evidence, every observed set of inputs loses money per order; fails runway test with about six months left at month 18 even on the plan's own numbers.
Recommended: break-even at about $11M of ARR, about two years out at 60% growth; profit within the cash and no capex, if hiring follows signed deals.

alternatives_considered.option: Sell store-based fast delivery to grocers
alternatives_considered.treatment: Chosen as step 3 (H2 2027): be the supplier of fast delivery to grocers rather than their competitor, without $5.4M of dark-store capex.

alternatives_considered.option: Copy Zipcart's fee and promotion fix
alternatives_considered.treatment: Would still leave the median store about $1 short per order (−$1.05) after a 14% volume loss; −$0.48 even with no volume loss.
Left out: the lead investor calls a round for a delivery operator unlikely; outside the board's control.

alternatives_considered.option: Rely on no Midwest rival building first
alternatives_considered.treatment: Left out: no city-level competitor data; the economics fail even with no rival.
Out of scope: the plan names Columbus, Indianapolis and Kansas City.
Reopen only when customer sites pass four re-entry tests, reviewed each January from 2028; all currently not met.

assumptions_and_uncertainties: The briefing pack holds no city-level data on rivals in Columbus, Indianapolis or Kansas City; "nobody owns the Midwest" is not tested
Incumbents' contribution per order is as each operator reports it; the pack does not define which costs it includes, so it is compared only loosely
Contribution excludes head office and launch marketing, so losses are understated
Best observed inputs combine best order value and best density from different sites; no site had both, so even this loss flatters
Zipcart fix assumes the fee carries no extra payment cost and riders keep 2.4 orders an hour at lower volume; in practice fewer orders would likely slow riders and deepen the loss
Rider pay held at $17.75 an hour; minimum pay rules under discussion in two of the three cities, size not yet known
A permanent store might do better than a temporary pop-up, but nothing in the pack shows by how much
Survey and pop-up cover different groups, so the gap shows intent against use rather than a like-for-like rate

Payback assumes retained customers keep ordering 3.1 times a month with no churn after month three; first two months' orders left out; store fixed costs not charged to the customer, which flatters the result
Acquisition estimate assumes Columbus behavior holds in all three cities, every customer won at $38, word of mouth not counted
